opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question we get a lot. In principle, one big multimodal model that does everything is very appealing, and long term that's probably where things converge. But in practice, when you look at how people actually use transcription, the requirements are pretty different from what you want in a general chat model.

The first thing is cost and latency. If you just want to turn hours of audio into text, running a very large model over every audio frame is a lot of compute you don't really need. A dedicated speech model can be much smaller and much faster for the same transcription quality. Customers care a lot about that, especially at scale: call centers, meeting transcription, media archives. They're processing huge volumes, and the price per hour of audio matters enormously.

The second thing is reliability. A big generalist model is trained to be helpful and to follow instructions, and sometimes that works against you in transcription. It might paraphrase, clean things up, or even respond to what's being said instead of just writing it down. For transcription you want something very faithful, very boring in a sense: exactly the words, the right timestamps, the right speaker. It's easier to get that behavior when the model is trained specifically for that task.

And third, modularity is just useful for developers. If you have a good transcription model, you can plug it in front of any text model, including one that's been fine-tuned for a specific domain, and you can swap pieces independently. You don't have to retrain or redeploy a giant multimodal system every time you want to improve one part.

That said, we definitely see value in native audio understanding inside larger models, for things like reasoning directly over tone, emotion, or very interactive voice use cases. So it's not either-or. For pure transcription, though, a specialized model is today the better trade-off.

r001.rationale: It says a dedicated speech model can be much smaller and faster while providing the same transcription quality.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the compute cost of running a very large model over audio with a dedicated model, and notes that the dedicated model matters for price per hour at scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it comes down to what you actually need the model to do. Transcription is a very well-defined task. You have audio in, text out, and you want it fast, cheap, and accurate across a lot of languages and acoustic conditions. A big multimodal model can do it, but you are paying for a lot of capability you don't use. You are running a model with tens or hundreds of billions of parameters to do something that a model with a few billion parameters can do just as well, and sometimes better, because it has been trained specifically for that.

The second thing is latency. If you want real-time transcription, streaming, something that works on-device or at the edge, you cannot afford a huge model in the loop. A dedicated speech model can be designed from the start for streaming, with the right architecture, the right chunking, the right tradeoff between delay and accuracy. When you bolt audio onto a large language model, you usually inherit the constraints of the language model, and streaming becomes an afterthought.

And then there is hallucination. Large language models are very good at producing plausible text, which is exactly what you don't want in transcription. If the audio is noisy or someone says something unusual, a language model will often "fix" it into something that sounds reasonable but was never said. A transcription model trained to stay close to the acoustic signal is much more faithful. For a lot of use cases, like meetings, medical, legal, you really want the model to write what was said, not what it thinks should have been said.

That doesn't mean the two are separate forever. Once you have a good transcription, you can hand it to the large model for understanding, summarization, reasoning, whatever you want. That modular setup is easier to evaluate, easier to improve one piece at a time, and much easier to deploy. Eventually, I think the models will converge, especially for things like speech-to-speech where you really want to preserve prosody and emotion that text throws away. But for transcription specifically, a focused model is just the right tool today.

r001.rationale: It says a model with a few billion parameters can do transcription “just as well” as one with tens or hundreds of billions.

r002.rationale: It says a large multimodal model makes you pay for capabilities you do not use, while describing transcription with a dedicated model as cheap.

astra-6.text:
For transcription, you have a very specific task: take the audio and turn it into text. You don’t necessarily need a large model that can also reason, write code, and understand images. A specialized model can be much smaller, faster, and cheaper to run.

Then you can pass the transcript to a language model if you need to do something more sophisticated. You only pay for that reasoning when you need it. Of course, you lose some information when you go through text—intonation, emotion—so there are cases where an integrated audio model makes sense. But for transcription alone, I think specialization is a very good tradeoff.

r001.rationale: The response says a specialized model can be smaller and more efficient, but does not state that it achieves essentially the same transcription performance as a large multimodal model.

r002.rationale: It says a specialized model is cheaper to run and contrasts it with a large multimodal model.

sol-6.1.text:
For transcription, you have a very well-defined task: you take audio and produce text. You can train a specialized model to do that very efficiently. You don’t necessarily need a huge model with all the capabilities of a general multimodal system just to recognize what someone said.

Then you can pass the transcript to a language model for reasoning or whatever you want to do next. You can improve the two components independently, and you don’t have to pay the cost of running the large model over all of the audio. Of course, you lose some information in the transcript—intonation, emotion—so it depends on the application. But if what you need is the words, I think a separate transcription model makes a lot of sense.

r001.rationale: The response says a specialized transcription model can handle the task efficiently, but does not claim it achieves essentially the same transcription performance as a large multimodal model.

r002.rationale: It says using a transcription model avoids paying the cost of running the large model over all the audio, clearly conveying a cost saving.
